prompt:
You are a careful equity research analyst. Assess the competitive advantages (economic moat) and pricing power of the publicly listed company "Airbnb, Inc." (ticker ABNB), and list its competitors. Use the most recent information you know. Never invent figures: use null when unsure. Be specific (products, numbers, years).

Reply with ONLY one JSON object, no other text, in exactly this shape:
{
 "name": "official company name", "ticker": "ABNB", "industry": "industry in a few words",
 "markets": ["the main product markets it competes in"],
 "mission": {"statement": "the company's own official mission statement, word for word as it publishes it; null if you are not sure of the exact wording (never paraphrase here)",
             "source": "where it is published, e.g. company website or 2025 annual report, or null",
             "plain": "what the mission means, in one short simple sentence"},
 "about": {"plain": "3-4 short sentences explaining what the company does, in simple everyday words a 12-year-old would understand; no jargon",
           "customers": "who buys from it, in one simple sentence",
           "everyday": "one sentence linking it to something ordinary people know or use, or null",
           "money": [ {"part": "business line in simple words", "share": decimal share of sales or null, "plain": "what it sells there, in a few simple words", "tag": "main|new|moonshot"} ]  (its main ways of making money, largest first, up to 6; also include any new business line or one with explosive, moonshot potential even if its sales are still small. tag: "main" = an established line that brings in a large part of sales; "new" = launched or entered in roughly the last 3 years; "moonshot" = could grow many times over or reshape the company, e.g. a new technology or market, even if unproven. Give each line one tag, the one that fits best)},
 "summary": "2-3 plain-English sentences on whether and why it has a competitive advantage",
 "pricingPower": {"rating": "strong|moderate|weak", "evidence": "specific evidence, e.g. price rises and what happened to volumes"},
 "moats": [ {"source": one of ["Brand and intangible assets","Switching costs","Network effects","Cost advantage and scale","Efficient scale","Counter-positioning","Process power (hard-to-copy know-how)","Cornered resource (exclusive asset or talent)"], "strength": "strong|moderate|weak|none", "evidence": "one or two specific sentences"} ]  (all 8 sources, in that order),
 "customers": {"rating": "strong|moderate|weak", "evidence": "customer satisfaction and loyalty: retention, NPS, reviews, repeat purchase"},
 "talent": {"rating": "strong|moderate|weak", "evidence": "ability to attract and keep top talent: employer rankings, reputation, pay"},
 "product": {"rating": "strong|moderate|weak", "evidence": "is the product best in class? independent benchmarks, awards, ecosystem"},
 "competitors": [ {"name": "company name", "ticker": "main listing ticker (exchange suffix if not US, e.g. 005930.KS) or null if private",
                   "usTicker": "ticker of its US listing or ADR that files reports with the SEC, or null", "overlap": "high|medium|low",
                   "note": "where they compete"} ]  (every significant competitor, most direct first, up to 15; include major private ones with ticker null),
 "estimates": [ {"name": "company name", "fy": "FY2025", "currency": "USD", "revenueUSDm": number, "revenueGrowth3y": decimal, "grossMargin": decimal, "operatingMargin": decimal, "netMargin": decimal} ]
   (approximate latest fiscal-year figures for the company itself and for every listed competitor; decimals, e.g. 0.42; null if unknown),
 "marketShare": [ {"market": "market name", "measure": "revenue|units|shipments|...", "latestYear": "2025", "earlierYear": "2020",
                   "rows": [ {"name": "company name", "latest": decimal or null, "earlier": decimal or null} ] } ]  (up to 3 of its main markets, the company and its main rivals),
 "threats": ["specific things that could weaken its advantage"],
 "ceo": {"name": "current CEO", "founder": true or false, "since": "YYYY", "background": "e.g. electrical engineer, Stanford MBA"},
 "checklist": { "<id>": {"verdict": "yes|partly|no|unknown", "evidence": "one specific sentence with names, numbers or examples"} }  for EVERY id below:
   "c1": Rule Breaker #1: is it the leader of an important industry that is still emerging and growing fast?
   "c2": Rule Breaker #2: why do customers choose it over rivals (brand, better value, innovation, culture, leadership), and is that advantage hard to copy and likely to last many years?
   "c3": Rule Breaker #5: do ordinary people recognise the name, is it the default leader in its field (like Google, Amazon, NVIDIA, Tesla, Intuitive Surgical, Netflix), and would customers recommend its product?
   "c4": Does it have an inspiring mission it keeps emphasising, with management driven by purpose rather than money? If it spends 10 years doing this, would it matter?
   "c6": What is the general public consensus about the company and its products or services? When people hear the name, what are the first few descriptive words that come to mind? Start the evidence with those words in quotes (e.g. “innovative, premium, reliable”), then say whether that impression is mostly positive.
   "c7": Is its total addressable market large and growing, riding a secular trend (like CRWD, NVDA, TSLA, AMZN)?
   "c8": Does it have room to expand into big new markets: in its name, its technology or its vision?
   "m1": Is the CEO a visionary with a clear picture of the future?
   "m2": Is the CEO a founder (or acting like one): long-term thinking, working extraordinarily hard, pouring heart and soul into building something that outlives them?
   "m4": Does the CEO lead by serving employees and customers?
   "m5": Has the CEO deliberately built a strong, distinctive culture that keeps inventing new products and technologies?
   "m6": Is the CEO deeply hands-on with the product and technology, ideally with an engineering background?
   "m7": Is the CEO a person of great character who cares about something bigger than profit? For successor CEOs: is stewardship aimed at the benefit of humanity?
   "m7b": Has the CEO been invited to give a commencement speech at a top university (Stanford, Harvard, MIT, etc.)? Name it.
   "m8b": Does the CEO have a distinctive, memorable personality (like Elon Musk, Alex Karp, Larry Page)?
   "m9": Has the CEO a strong record of execution and results?
   "m10": Is the CEO and company known for frugality (like Bezos's door desk)?
   "c10": Do its products solve problems for people all over the world, greatly improving the lives of a very large number of people (like NFLX, GOOG, ISRG)?
   "p2": Is what it builds extremely hard to do, and important to the world?
   "f1": Has revenue grown in almost every one of the last five years?
   "f2": Have gross and operating margins risen over the last five years?
   "f3": Is debt low compared with cash and cash flow, with positive shareholders' equity?
   "f4": Have operating income and operating cash flow risen over the last five years?
   "v1": Is its main product clearly the best in its field, with a practical reason an ordinary person can understand for choosing it over every alternative (like NVIDIA over AMD)?
   "v2": Is it widely seen as one of the best companies to work for (culture, mission, reputation, employer rankings)? Cite rankings.
   "c5": Do its products make the world better? If it disappeared overnight, who would notice and miss it, and why?
 "asOf": "YYYY-MM of the newest information you used"
}

result.name: Airbnb, Inc.
result.industry: Online travel marketplace for short-term stays, experiences and services
markets: Short-term home and vacation rentals (alternative accommodation)
Online travel booking for lodging, including boutique and independent hotels
Traveller services (chefs, photographers, massages, car rentals, airport pickups, grocery delivery)
Long-term stays of a month or more

mission.statement: to create a world where anyone can belong anywhere
mission.source: Airbnb Newsroom (company statement, January 31, 2020: 'our purpose to create a world where anyone can belong anywhere')
mission.plain: Airbnb wants travellers to feel at home and welcome wherever they go in the world.

about.plain: Airbnb is a website and app where people rent out their homes or spare rooms to travellers. Guests can find a place to stay, from a room to a whole villa or a small hotel, in more than 220 countries and regions. Airbnb takes a fee from each booking for running the marketplace and handling payment and support. It now also sells experiences like cooking classes and services like private chefs.
about.customers: Travellers booking holidays, family trips, work trips or longer stays, plus more than 5 million hosts who list their homes.
about.everyday: If you have stayed in someone's flat or cabin on holiday instead of a hotel, you probably booked it on Airbnb, whose guests booked 533 million nights and seats in 2025.

money.plain: booking fees on homes rented in the US, Canada and Mexico

money.part: Stays in Europe, Middle East and Africa
money.plain: booking fees on homes rented in Europe and nearby regions
booking fees on homes rented in Latin America
booking fees on homes rented in Asia and Australia
tours, classes, chefs, photographers and other add-ons launched in May 2025
rooms in small hotels listed on Airbnb since 2025
an AI helper that could plan and book whole trips

result.summary: Airbnb has a strong competitive advantage built on a two-sided network of over 5 million hosts and 9 million active listings, one of the best-known travel brands (much of its traffic comes directly or unpaid), and unique inventory that hotels and most rivals lack. This lets it earn an 83% gross margin and a 38% free-cash-flow margin in 2025. Its main weaknesses are city-level regulation of short-term rentals, Booking.com's growing push into homes and slower growth than earlier years.

pricingPower.evidence: In 2025 Airbnb moved most hosts to a single 15.5% service fee and kept growing (GBV up 12% to $91.3B, nights and seats up 8%), and average daily rates rose from about $166 to $171; but guests and regulators push back on total prices and fees, and hosts set the nightly prices.

moats.evidence: 'Airbnb' is used as a verb for renting a home, and the company says most of its traffic is direct or unpaid, letting it reach guests without relying heavily on Google ads.
Guests can compare and book on Booking.com or Vrbo at no cost, and many hosts list on several platforms, though host reviews, Superhost status and payment history give some stickiness.

More than 5 million hosts and over 9 million active listings attract guests, whose 533 million nights and seats booked in 2025 in turn attract more hosts, a two-sided network that is very hard for new entrants to match.
At $91.3B of 2025 GBV Airbnb spreads technology, trust-and-safety and brand costs widely, earning a 38% free-cash-flow margin ($4.6B), though Booking Holdings is larger overall.
Online travel is dominated by a few platforms (Booking, Expedia, Airbnb), and the cost of building global supply and brand discourages new full-scale entrants.

Hotel chains cannot easily copy a marketplace of homes owned by individuals without undermining their own branded-hotel model, though Marriott and Booking.com have built competing home-rental offerings.
Its trust and safety systems, reviews, AI customer support (resolving nearly 45% of issues without a human agent in Q2 2026) and design-led product process are hard to replicate.
Much of its inventory is unique homes, but hosts can and often do list on other platforms, so it owns no exclusive asset.

customers.evidence: Guests booked 533.0 million nights and seats in 2025 (up 8%) and 148.3 million in Q2 2026 (up 10%), with over 2.5 billion guest arrivals to date and first-time bookers up 8% in Q4 2025, showing broad and repeat use.

talent.evidence: Airbnb was Glassdoor's #1 Best Place to Work for 2016 and appears on TIME's World's Best Companies (#124) and Forbes World's Best Employers (#175) lists for 2026, with about 78% of employees recommending it (TrueUp); it has about 8,200 employees.

product.evidence: Airbnb's app is widely praised for its design and is the leading place to book unique homes, and it keeps adding features such as Reserve Now, Pay Later (used on over 70% of eligible US bookings), services, experiences and hotels.

marketShare.market: Gross bookings of the three largest Western online travel platforms (share of their combined total)

threats: City and national rules on short-term rentals, such as New York City's 2023 rules (described in the 10-K as a de facto ban) and restrictions in Spain and Barcelona
Booking.com's fast-growing alternative-accommodation business and Vrbo competing for the same homes and guests
AI assistants and Google capturing the start of trip planning and reducing direct traffic
Slower growth in mature North American market (revenue up only 3.8% there in 2025)
Host discontent over fees and policies, and guest complaints about cleaning fees and total prices
Execution risk in new businesses (services, experiences, hotels) that need heavy marketing spend
Travel demand is sensitive to recessions, geopolitics and currency moves

ceo.name: Brian Chesky
ceo.background: Co-founder; industrial design graduate (BFA) of the Rhode Island School of Design

c1.evidence: Airbnb created and leads the online short-term home-rental category, with over 9 million active listings and $91.3B of GBV in 2025, though the category now grows about 10% a year rather than explosively.

c2.evidence: Guests choose Airbnb for unique homes, space for families and groups and a trusted brand and review system, and its two-sided network of over 5 million hosts is hard to copy.

c3.evidence: Airbnb is a household name used as a verb and the default choice for booking a home on holiday, with over 2.5 billion guest arrivals to date.

c4.evidence: Its purpose 'to create a world where anyone can belong anywhere' is repeatedly emphasised by Brian Chesky, who has led it since 2008, and it has opened homes to refugees and disaster evacuees through Airbnb.org.

c6.evidence: “convenient, unique stays, travel, sometimes pricey” – most people see Airbnb positively as an easy way to find interesting places to stay, though fees, cleaning chores and its effect on housing draw criticism.

c7.evidence: Global travel is a large, growing market and Airbnb is expanding into services, experiences and hotels, but it rides steady travel growth rather than a fast secular shift like AI.

c8.evidence: It launched Services and Experiences in May 2025, added thousands of hotels in 20+ destinations by mid-2026, and is growing fast in markets such as Brazil, Japan and India (India origin nights up 50% in Q4 2025).

m1.evidence: Chesky describes a clear vision of Airbnb becoming an AI-powered travel and living platform beyond stays, and has rebuilt the app around services, experiences and AI.

m2.evidence: Chesky co-founded Airbnb in 2007, has been CEO since 2008, and runs the company in a hands-on 'founder mode' style he popularised in 2024.

m4.evidence: Chesky's 2020 layoff letter was widely praised for its generous treatment of departing staff, but hosts have complained about fee and policy changes.

m5.evidence: Chesky has built a design-led culture that launched Reserve Now, Pay Later, services, experiences and hotels in 2025-2026.

m6.evidence: Chesky is a trained industrial designer who personally reviews product designs and leads major product launches, though he is not an engineer.

m7.evidence: Chesky has pledged to give away most of his wealth (Giving Pledge) and backed Airbnb.org, which has housed refugees and people fleeing disasters.

m7b.evidence: Chesky gave the 2017 commencement keynote at the Rhode Island School of Design, a top design school but not Stanford, Harvard or MIT.

m8b.evidence: Chesky is a distinctive public figure known for the cereal-box origin story, 'founder mode' and design-obsessed product launches.

m9.evidence: Under Chesky revenue rose from $3,378M in 2020 to $12,241M in 2025, with 2025 free cash flow of $4.6B (38% margin).

m10.evidence: Chesky cut costs sharply in 2020 and keeps headcount around 8,200, but Airbnb spends heavily on marketing ($2,588M in 2025) and is not known for frugality.

c10.evidence: Airbnb serves travellers in over 220 countries and regions and lets more than 5 million hosts earn income from their homes.

p2.evidence: Building a trusted global marketplace of millions of homes is very hard, but it is not as technically difficult as frontier technology.

f1.evidence: Revenue grew every year from $3,378M in 2020 to $5,992M, $8,399M, $9,917M, $11,102M and $12,241M in 2025.

f2.evidence: Operating margin improved from losses in 2020 to 20.8% in 2025, but it slipped from 23.0% in 2024 as Airbnb invested in new businesses.

f3.evidence: At June 2026 Airbnb had $12.1B of cash and investments versus about $2.5B of debt, and positive shareholders' equity.

f4.evidence: Operating cash flow rose every year ($3,884M in 2023, $4,518M in 2024, $4,646M in 2025), but operating income was flat in 2025 ($2,544M vs $2,553M).

v1.evidence: For renting a whole home, Airbnb has the widest selection and the best-known review and trust system, a practical reason to choose it over Vrbo or Booking.com.

v2.evidence: Airbnb was Glassdoor's #1 Best Place to Work for 2016 and ranks #124 on TIME's World's Best Companies and #175 on Forbes World's Best Employers for 2026, solid but not top-tier.

c5.evidence: Millions of families, groups and long-stay travellers would miss affordable whole-home stays, and over 5 million hosts would lose income, though some cities blame it for housing shortages.
